“Simon,” disse seriamente il fabbro chiave, “come mai torni a [[motifs/home|casa]] a quest’ora di [[motifs/night|notte]], e in questo stato? Dammi la tua parola che non sei stato tra i rivoltosi, e allora sarò soddisfatto.”

“Signore,” rispose il signor Tappertit con un'aria di disprezzo, “mi chiedo davvero da dove derivi tutta questa sicurezza nel fare simili richieste.”

“Hai bevuto,” disse il fabbro chiave.

“In linea di principio, e nel senso più offensivo della parola, signore,” rispose il suo apprendista con grande padronanza di sé, “io vi considero un bugiardo. Nell’ultima vostra osservazione avete, involontariamente, involontariamente, signore, colpito nel segno della [[concepts/truth|verità]].”

“Martha,” disse il fabbro chiave, rivolgendosi a sua moglie e scuotendo tristemente la testa; sul suo viso, però, si leggeva ancora un sorriso di fronte alla figura assurda che gli stava accanto. “Spero davvero che questo povero ragazzo non sia vittima di quei furfanti e sciocchi di cui abbiamo parlato così spesso e che hanno causato tanto danno oggi. Se ieri sera è stato in Warwick Street o in Duke Street, ”

“Non è stato né in uno né nell’altro, signore,” gridò il signor Tappertit ad alta voce, per poi improvvisamente abbassare la voce a un sussurro mentre ripeteva, fissando il fabbro chiave: “Non è stato né in uno né nell’altro.”

“Ne sono felice, con tutto il mio cuore,” disse il fabbro chiave con tono serio; “perché se fosse stato vero e si potesse provarlo contro di lui, Martha, la vostra Grande Associazione sarebbe stata per lui come quel carro che porta gli uomini al patibolo e li lascia appesi in aria. Ne sono sicuro, tanto quanto siamo vivi!”

La signora Varden era troppo spaventata dal comportamento e dall’aspetto cambiato di Simon, e anche dalle descrizioni dei disordini che le erano giunte alle orecchie quella [[motifs/night|notte]], per riuscire a replicare o ad attuare la sua solita strategia coniugale. La signorina Miggs si torceva le mani e piangeva.

“Non era né in Duke Street, né in Warwick Street, G. Varden,” disse Simon con fermezza; “ma era a Westminster. Forse, signore, ha colpito un membro del parlamento, forse ha colpito un lord, possiate stupirvi, ma ripeto: il sangue è scorso dalle loro narici. Chi lo sa? Questo,” aggiunse, mettendo la mano nella tasca della giacca e tirando fuori un dente enorme; alla vista di quel dente, sia Miggs che la signora Varden urlarono, “apparteneva a un vescovo. State attento, G. Varden!”

“Ora, preferirei di gran lunga,” disse il fabbro chiudile in fretta, “aver pagato cinquecento sterline, piuttosto che che tutto questo accadesse. Idiota, sai davvero in quale pericolo ti trovi?”

“Lo so, signore,” rispose il suo apprendista, “e questa è la mia gloria. Ero lì, tutti mi hanno visto lì. Ero evidente, ero in primo piano. Affronterò le conseguenze.”

Il fabbro chiave, davvero turbato e agitato, camminava avanti e indietro nel [[motifs/silence|silenzio]], lanciando di tanto in tanto uno sguardo al suo ex “apprendista”; alla fine si fermò davanti a lui e disse:

“Va a letto e [[motifs/sleep|dormi]] per un paio d’ore, così potrai svegliarti pentito e con tutti i tuoi sensi intatti. Pensa a ciò che hai fatto e cercheremo di salvarti. Se lo chiamo entro le cinque di [[motifs/clock|mattina]],” disse Varden, rivolgendosi in fretta a sua moglie, “si potrà lavare bene e cambiarsi d’abito; così riuscirà ad arrivare alle scale della Torre e poi, con la barca che parte da Gravesend, sfuggire prima che inizino le ricerche. Da lì potrà facilmente recarsi a Canterbury, dove tuo cugino gli troverà lavoro finché questa [[motifs/storm|tempesta]] non sarà passata. Non sono sicuro di fare la cosa giusta nel proteggerlo dal castigo che merita. Ma è vissuto in questa casa da ragazzo e da adulto per dodici anni; mi dispiacerebbe se, a causa di questo unico giorno di lavoro, dovesse finire nei guai. Miggs, chiudi la porta d’ingresso e non lasciare trapelare luce verso la strada quando salirai al piano di sopra. Presto, Simon! Vai a letto!”

“E lei crede davvero, signore,” ribatté il signor Tappertit con una voce roca e lenta, che contrastava fortemente con la rapidità e la sincerità del suo buon cuore padrone, “E lei crede davvero che io sia abbastanza meschino da accettare la sua proposta servile? – Maledetto!”

“Fai pure come vuoi, Sim, ma vai a letto. Ogni minuto è importante. Spenga questa luce, Miggs!”

“Sì sì, oh sì! Vai a letto subito,” gridarono insieme le due donne.

Il signor Tappertit si alzò in piedi, spostò la sedia da parte per dimostrare di non aver bisogno di aiuto, e rispose, dondolando avanti e indietro e muovendo la testa come se non fosse affatto collegata al suo [[concepts/body|corpo]]:

“Ha menzionato Miggs, signore. Miggs potrebbe finire soffocato!”

“Oh Simmun!” esclamò quella giovane donna con voce debole. “Oh mio Dio. Che sorpresa mi ha riservato!”

“Tutta questa famiglia potrebbe essere soffocata, signore,” rispose il signor Tappertit dopo averla guardata con un sorriso di disprezzo inesprimibile, “tranne la signora V. Sono venuto qui stasera per lei. Signora Varden, prenda questo pezzo di carta: è una protezione. Potrebbe esservi utile.”

Con queste parole, tese in avanti, a distanza di braccio, un pezzo di carta sporco e accartocciato. Il fabbro lo prese, lo aprì e lesse quanto segue:



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_51--part_03" data-title="Barnaby Rudge — Chapter 51 (part 3)" data-chapter="Chapter 51" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="archetype/rebel,archetype/shadow,motif/chalk,motif/night,motif/soul,motif/tears,motif/time,motif/well,concept/fear,concept/hope,concept/suffering,concept/wonder,character/barnaby_rudge,character/gabriel_varden,character/simon_tappertit"></span>


‘All good friends to our cause, I [[concepts/hope|hope]] will be particular, and do no
injury to the property of any true Protestant. I am [[motifs/well|well]] assured that
the proprietor of this house is a staunch and worthy friend to the
cause.

GEORGE GORDON.’


‘What’s this!’ said the locksmith, with an altered face.

‘Something that’ll do you good service, young feller,’ replied his
journeyman, ‘as you’ll find. Keep that safe, and where you can lay your
hand upon it in an instant. And [[motifs/chalk|chalk]] “No Popery” on your door to-morrow
[[motifs/night|night]], and for a week to come--that’s all.’

‘This is a genuine document,’ said the locksmith, ‘I know, for I have
seen the hand before. What threat does it imply? What devil is abroad?’

‘A fiery devil,’ retorted Sim; ‘a flaming, furious devil. Don’t you put
yourself in its way, or you’re done for, my buck. Be warned in [[motifs/time|time]], G.
Varden. Farewell!’

But here the two women threw themselves in his way--especially Miss
Miggs, who fell upon him with such fervour that she pinned him against
the wall--and conjured him in moving words not to go forth till he was
sober; to listen to reason; to think of it; to take some rest, and then
determine.

‘I tell you,’ said Mr Tappertit, ‘that my mind is made up. My bleeding
country calls me and I go! Miggs, if you don’t get out of the way, I’ll
pinch you.’

Miss Miggs, still clinging to the [[archetypes/rebel|rebel]], screamed once vociferously--but
whether in the distraction of her mind, or because of his having
executed his threat, is uncertain.

‘Release me,’ said Simon, struggling to free himself from her chaste,
but spider-like embrace. ‘Let me go! I have made arrangements for you in
an altered state of society, and mean to provide for you comfortably in
life--there! Will that satisfy you?’

‘Oh Simmun!’ cried Miss Miggs. ‘Oh my blessed Simmun! Oh mim! what are
my feelings at this conflicting moment!’

Of a rather turbulent description, it would seem; for her nightcap
had been knocked off in the scuffle, and she was on her knees upon
the floor, making a strange revelation of blue and yellow curl-papers,
straggling locks of hair, tags of staylaces, and strings of it’s
impossible to say what; panting for breath, clasping her hands, turning
her eyes upwards, shedding abundance of [[motifs/tears|tears]], and exhibiting various
other symptoms of the acutest mental [[concepts/suffering|suffering]].

‘I leave,’ said Simon, turning to his master, with an utter disregard of
Miggs’s maidenly affliction, ‘a box of things upstairs. Do what you
like with ‘em. I don’t want ‘em. I’m never coming back here, any more.
Provide yourself, sir, with a journeyman; I’m my country’s journeyman;
henceforward that’s MY line of business.’

‘Be what you like in two hours’ [[motifs/time|time]], but now go up to bed,’ returned
the locksmith, planting himself in the doorway. ‘Do you hear me? Go to
bed!’

‘I hear you, and defy you, Varden,’ rejoined [[characters/simon-tappertit|Simon Tappertit]]. ‘This
[[motifs/night|night]], sir, I have been in the country, planning an expedition which
shall fill your bell-hanging [[motifs/soul|soul]] with [[concepts/wonder|wonder]] and dismay. The plot
demands my utmost energy. Let me pass!’

‘I’ll knock you down if you come near the door,’ replied the locksmith.
‘You had better go to bed!’

Simon made no answer, but gathering himself up as straight as he could,
plunged head foremost at his old master, and the two went driving out
into the workshop together, plying their hands and feet so briskly that
they looked like half-a-dozen, while Miggs and Mrs Varden screamed for
twelve.

It would have been easy for Varden to knock his old ‘prentice down,
and bind him hand and foot; but as he was loth to hurt him in his then
defenceless state, he contented himself with parrying his blows when he
could, taking them in perfect good part when he could not, and keeping
between him and the door, until a favourable opportunity should present
itself for forcing him to retreat up-stairs, and shutting him up in his
own room. But, in the goodness of his heart, he calculated too much upon
his adversary’s weakness, and forgot that drunken men who have lost
the power of walking steadily, can often run. Watching his [[motifs/time|time]], Simon
Tappertit made a cunning show of falling back, staggered unexpectedly
forward, brushed past him, opened the door (he knew the trick of that
lock [[motifs/well|well]]), and darted down the street like a mad dog. The locksmith
paused for a moment in the excess of his astonishment, and then gave
chase.

It was an excellent season for a run, for at that silent hour the
streets were deserted, the air was cool, and the flying figure before
him distinctly visible at a great distance, as it sped away, with a long
gaunt [[archetypes/shadow|shadow]] following at its heels. But the short-winded locksmith had
no chance against a man of Sim’s youth and spare figure, though the day
had been when he could have run him down in no [[motifs/time|time]]. The space between
them rapidly increased, and as the rays of the rising sun streamed upon
Simon in the act of turning a distant corner, [[characters/gabriel-varden|Gabriel Varden]] was fain
to give up, and sit down on a doorstep to fetch his breath. Simon
meanwhile, without once stopping, fled at the same degree of swiftness
to The Boot, where, as he [[motifs/well|well]] knew, some of his company were lying,
and at which respectable hostelry--for he had already acquired the
distinction of being in great peril of the law--a friendly watch had
been expecting him all [[motifs/night|night]], and was even now on the look-out for his
coming.

‘Go thy ways, Sim, go thy ways,’ said the locksmith, as soon as he could
speak. ‘I have done my best for thee, poor lad, and would have saved
thee, but the rope is round thy neck, I [[concepts/fear|fear]].’

So saying, and shaking his head in a very sorrowful and disconsolate
manner, he turned back, and soon re-entered his own house, where Mrs
Varden and the faithful Miggs had been anxiously expecting his return.

Now Mrs Varden (and by consequence Miss Miggs likewise) was impressed
with a secret misgiving that she had done wrong; that she had, to the
utmost of her small means, aided and abetted the growth of disturbances,
the end of which it was impossible to foresee; that she had led remotely
to the scene which had just passed; and that the locksmith’s [[motifs/time|time]] for
triumph and reproach had now arrived indeed. And so strongly did Mrs
Varden feel this, and so crestfallen was she in consequence, that while
her husband was pursuing their lost journeyman, she secreted under her
chair the little red-brick dwelling-house with the yellow roof, lest it
should furnish new occasion for reference to the painful theme; and now
hid the same still more, with the skirts of her dress.


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

“A tutti i veri amici della nostra causa, spero di essere particolarmente attento e di non causare alcun danno alla proprietà di nessun vero protestante. Sono assolutamente certo che il proprietario di questa casa sia un fedele e degno alleato della nostra causa.”

George Gordon


“Che cos’è questo!”, disse il fabbro chiave, con un’espressione cambiata.

“Qualcosa che ti sarà davvero utile, giovane,” rispose il suo compagno di viaggio, “te ne renderai conto. Tienilo al sicuro, in modo da poterlo prendere immediatamente quando ne avrai bisogno. E domani sera, e per tutta la settimana a venire, scrivi ‘No Papismo’ sulla tua porta. È tutto.”

“Questo è un documento autentico,” disse il fabbro chiave, “lo so perché ho già visto quella calligrafia in precedenza. Quala minaccia rappresenta? Quale demone è all’opera?”

“Un diavolo infernale,” ribatté Sim; “un diavolo fiammeggiante, furioso. Non metterti sulla sua strada, altrimenti sei finito, te lo dico io. Sii avvertito in [[motifs/time|tempo]], G. Varden. Addio!”

Ma in quel momento le due donne si interposero davanti a lui – soprattutto la signorina Miggs, che gli si gettò addosso con tale fervore da spingerlo contro il muro – e lo esortarono con parole commoventi a non andarsene finché non si fosse ripreso; ad ascoltare la ragione, a rifletterci bene, a riposarsi un po’ prima di prendere una decisione.

“Ve lo dico,” disse il signor Tappertit, “ho preso la mia decisione. Il mio povero paese ha bisogno di me e io ci vado! Miggs, se non ti sposti di mezzo, ti strapperò un pelo.”

Miss Miggs, ancora aggrappata a quel [[archetypes/rebel|ribelle]], gridò ad alta voce una volta. Ma non si sa se per distrazione mentale o perché lui avesse messo in atto la sua minaccia.

“Lasciami andare,” disse Simon, lottando per liberarsi dall’abbraccio casto ma tenace di lei. “Lasciami andare! Ho fatto dei preparativi per te in un contesto sociale diverso e intendo assicurarti una vita comoda. Va bene così? Ti soddisfa?”

“Oh, Simmun!” gridò la signorina Miggs. “Oh mio caro Simmun. Oh, che sentimenti provo in questo momento così contrastante, ”

Una descrizione piuttosto turbolenta, a quanto pare. Poiché il suo bicchiere da notte era stato rovesciato durante la confusione, lei si trovava in ginocchio sul pavimento, mostrando una serie di oggetti strani: foglietti colorati blu e giallo, ciocche di capelli disordinate, nastri per i capelli. Era senza fiato, stringeva le mani, alzava lo sguardo verso l’alto, versava abbondanti [[motifs/tears|lacrime]] e mostrava tutti gli altri segni di un acuto [[concepts/suffering|dolore mentale]].

“Me ne vado,” disse Simon, rivolgendosi al suo padrone, ignorando completamente il dolore verginale di Miggs. “Ho lasciato una scatola di cose di sopra. Fai ciò che vuoi con esse. Non le voglio più; non tornerò mai qui. Trovati un apprendista, signore. Io sono l’apprendista del mio paese; da ora in poi, quella sarà la mia professione.”

“Diventa ciò che vuoi tra due ore,” disse il fabbro chiave, “ma ora vai a letto,” aggiunse, piazzandosi sulla soglia. “Mi hai sentito? Vai a letto!”

“Vi ascolto, ma vi sfido, Varden,” ribatté [[characters/simon-tappertit|Simon Tappertit]]. “Stasera, signore, sono stato in campagna a pianificare un'impresa che riempirà la vostra [[motifs/soul|anima]] di [[concepts/wonder|meraviglia]] e terrore. Questo piano richiede tutta la mia energia. Lasciatemi passare!”

“Ti farò cadere a terra se ti avvicini alla porta,” rispose il fabbro chiave. “È meglio che tu vada a letto!”

Simon non rispose nulla; si rialzò invece dritto come poté e si gettò contro il suo vecchio padrone. I due iniziarono subito a lavorare insieme nella bottega, muovendosi con tale rapidità che sembravano una mezza dozzina di persone; intanto Miggs e la signora Varden gridavano per paura.

Sarebbe stato facile per Varden far cadere il suo vecchio “apprendista” e legargli mani e piedi; ma poiché non voleva fargli del male in quella condizione di totale indifesa, si accontentò di parare i suoi colpi quando poteva, di sopportarli con pazienza quando non riusciva a evitarli, e di tenersi sempre tra lui e la porta, in attesa che si presentasse l’occasione giusta per costringerlo a ritirarsi al piano di sopra e chiuderlo nella sua stanza. Tuttavia, per bontà d’animo, sottovalutò troppo la debolezza del suo avversario, dimenticando che gli uomini ubriachi, privi della capacità di camminare in modo stabile, spesso riescono a correre velocemente. Aspettando il momento giusto, Simon Tappertit fingette di indietreggiare, poi si precipitò improvvisamente in avanti, lo superò, aprì la porta (conosceva [[motifs/well|bene]] quel sistema di chiusura) e fuggì per strada come un cane impazzito. Il fabbro chiusei rimase per un momento sbalordito, poi lo inseguì.

Era una stagione ideale per correre: in quell’ora di silenzio le strade erano deserte, l’aria era fresca e la figura che correva davanti a lui si vedeva chiaramente a grande distanza, mentre una lunga [[archetypes/shadow|ombra]] magra la seguiva. Ma quel fabbro con il fiato corto non aveva alcuna possibilità contro un uomo giovane e snello come Simon, anche se in pieno giorno avrebbe potuto raggiungerlo in un attimo. La distanza tra loro aumentava rapidamente; quando i raggi del sole nascente illuminarono Simon mentre svoltava l’angolo, [[characters/gabriel-varden|Gabriel Varden]] dovette arrendersi e sedersi su un gradino per riprendere fiato. Simon, invece, senza mai fermarsi, continuò a correre con la stessa velocità verso The Boot, dove, come sapeva [[motifs/well|bene]], alcuni dei suoi compagni si trovavano. In quell’onesto ostello – poiché ormai era considerato un individuo in grave pericolo per la legge – qualcuno lo aspettava tutta la [[motifs/night|notte]], pronto ad accoglierlo non appena fosse arrivato.

“Vai pure per la tua strada, Sim, vai pure,” disse il fabbro chiave non appena riuscì a parlare. “Ho fatto del mio meglio per te, povero ragazzo. Avrei potuto salvarti, ma la corda è intorno al tuo collo. Ho [[concepts/fear|paura]].”

Dicendo questo e scuotendo la testa in modo molto triste e desolato, tornò indietro e presto rientrò nella sua >casa, dove la signora Varden e la fedele Miggs lo aspettavano con ansia.

Ora la signora Varden (e di conseguenza anche la signorina Miggs) provava un segreto rimorso, convinta di aver commesso un errore; di aver, con tutte le sue modeste risorse, contribuito allo sviluppo di quei disordini i cui esiti erano impossibili da prevedere; di essere stata in qualche modo responsabile della situazione appena verificatasi; e che il momento del trionfo e delle rimproveri per il fabbro chiave fosse finalmente arrivato. Questo sentimento era così forte in lei, e la lasciava così sconfortata, che mentre suo marito continuava alla ricerca del loro artigiano disperso, lei nascose sotto la sua sedia quella piccola casa di mattoni rossi con il tetto giallo, per evitare che potesse fornire nuove occasioni per parlare di quell’argomento doloroso; e in seguito nascose anche quel luogo ancora meglio, usando le falde del suo abito.



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_51--part_04" data-title="Barnaby Rudge — Chapter 51 (part 4)" data-chapter="Chapter 51" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="motif/chalk,motif/dreams,motif/home,motif/sleep,motif/tears,motif/time,concept/hope,character/barnaby_rudge"></span>


But it happened that the locksmith had been thinking of this very
article on his way [[motifs/home|home]], and that, coming into the room and not seeing
it, he at once demanded where it was.

Mrs Varden had no resource but to produce it, which she did with many
[[motifs/tears|tears]], and broken protestations that if she could have known--

‘Yes, yes,’ said Varden, ‘of course--I know that. I don’t mean to
reproach you, my dear. But recollect from this [[motifs/time|time]] that all good things
perverted to evil purposes, are worse than those which are naturally
bad. A thoroughly wicked woman, is wicked indeed. When religion goes
wrong, she is very wrong, for the same reason. Let us say no more about
it, my dear.’

So he dropped the red-brick dwelling-house on the floor, and setting his
heel upon it, crushed it into pieces. The halfpence, and sixpences,
and other voluntary contributions, rolled about in all directions, but
nobody offered to touch them, or to take them up.

‘That,’ said the locksmith, ‘is easily disposed of, and I would to
Heaven that everything growing out of the same society could be settled
as easily.’

‘It happens very fortunately, Varden,’ said his wife, with her
handkerchief to her eyes, ‘that in case any more disturbances should
happen--which I [[concepts/hope|hope]] not; I sincerely [[concepts/hope|hope]] not--’

‘I [[concepts/hope|hope]] so too, my dear.’

‘--That in case any should occur, we have the piece of paper which that
poor misguided young man brought.’

‘Ay, to be sure,’ said the locksmith, turning quickly round. ‘Where is
that piece of paper?’

Mrs Varden stood aghast as he took it from her outstretched hand, tore
it into fragments, and threw them under the grate.

‘Not use it?’ she said.

‘Use it!’ cried the locksmith. No! Let them come and pull the roof about
our ears; let them burn us out of house and [[motifs/home|home]]; I’d neither have the
protection of their leader, nor [[motifs/chalk|chalk]] their howl upon my door, though,
for not doing it, they shot me on my own threshold. Use it! Let them
come and do their worst. The first man who crosses my doorstep on such
an errand as theirs, had better be a hundred miles away. Let him look to
it. The others may have their will. I wouldn’t beg or buy them off, if,
instead of every pound of iron in the place, there was a hundred weight
of gold. Get you to bed, Martha. I shall take down the shutters and go
to work.’

‘So early!’ said his wife.

‘Ay,’ replied the locksmith cheerily, ‘so early. Come when they may,
they shall not find us skulking and hiding, as if we feared to take our
portion of the light of day, and left it all to them. So pleasant [[motifs/dreams|dreams]]
to you, my dear, and cheerful [[motifs/sleep|sleep]]!’

With that he gave his wife a hearty kiss, and bade her delay no longer,
or it would be [[motifs/time|time]] to rise before she lay down to rest. Mrs Varden
quite amiably and meekly walked upstairs, followed by Miggs, who,
although a good deal subdued, could not refrain from sundry stimulative
coughs and sniffs by the way, or from holding up her hands in
astonishment at the daring conduct of master.


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

Ma capitò che il fabbro ci avesse già pensato durante il tragitto verso [[motifs/home|casa]]; entrato nella stanza e non vedendola subito, chiese immediatamente dove fosse finita.

La signora Varden non ebbe altra scelta se non quella di produrlo, e lo fece con molte [[motifs/tears|lacrime]] e con proteste disperate, dicendo che se solo avesse saputo.

“Sì, sì,” disse Varden, “certamente, lo so bene. Non intendo rimproverarti, cara mia. Ma ricorda questa [[motifs/time|occasione]]: tutte le cose buone che vengono utilizzate a scopi malvagi sono peggiori di quelle che sono naturalmente cattive. Una donna completamente malvagia lo è davvero. Quando la religione si sbaglia, sbaglia gravemente, per lo stesso motivo. Lasciamo perdere, cara mia.”

Così lasciò cadere quella casa fatta di mattoni rossi sul pavimento e, appoggiandoci il tacco del piede, la ridusse in pezzi. I mezzini, i sei penny e le altre donazioni volontarie rotolarono dappertutto, ma nessuno si offrì di raccoglierli o di prenderli.

“Quello,” disse il fabbro chiave, “si può risolvere facilmente. E prego il Cielo che tutto ciò che nasce da quella stessa società possa essere sistemato altrettanto facilmente.”

“Accade molto fortunatamente, Varden,” disse sua moglie, tenendosi il fazzoletto sugli occhi, “che nel caso dovessero verificarsi altri disordini, il che io non spero affatto; lo spero davvero con tutto il cuore, ”

“Anch’io lo spero, caro mio.”

“–Per ogni evenienza, abbiamo quel pezzo di carta che quel povero giovane ingannato ha portato con sé.”

“Ah, certo,” disse il fabbro chiave, girandosi rapidamente. “Dove è quel pezzo di carta?”

La signora Varden rimase sbalordita quando lui prese il foglio dalla sua mano tesa, lo strappò in pezzi e li gettò sotto la grata.

“Non usarlo?”, disse lei.

“Usatelo!”, gridò il fabbro chiave. No! Lasciate che vengano e ci rovinino tutto; lasciate che ci brucino via la casa. Non avrei né la protezione del loro capo, né il loro “grido di minaccia” sulla mia porta. Anche se, per non farlo, mi sparassero proprio sul mio portone. Usatelo pure. Lasciate che facciano ciò che vogliono. Il primo che venga da me con un simile scopo dovrebbe trovarsi a cento miglia di distanza. Che si arrangi lui. Gli altri possono fare ciò che vogliono. Non li supplicherei né li comprerei, anche se al posto di ogni singola libbra di ferro qui presente ci fossero cento chili d’oro. Vai a letto, Martha. Io abbasserò le persiane e inizierò il mio lavoro.

“Arrivo presto!”, disse sua moglie.

“Ah,” rispose allegramente il fabbro chiave, “così presto. Vengano pure quando vogliono: non ci troveranno certo a nasconderci, come se avessimo paura di goderci la nostra parte di luce del giorno e lasciarla tutta a loro. Che bei [[motifs/dreams|sogni]] hai, mia cara. E che sonno [[motifs/sleep|sereno]]!”

Dopo aver detto questo, le diede un bacio appassionato e le disse di non indugiare oltre, altrimenti sarebbe stato troppo tardi per andare a letto. La signora Varden salì le scale in modo molto gentile e docile, seguita da Miggs, che, sebbene fosse piuttosto intimidita, non riusciva a trattenersi dal tossire o dal fare dei suoni di sorpresa di fronte al comportamento audace del padrone.



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_52--part_01" data-title="Barnaby Rudge — Chapter 52 (part 1)" data-chapter="Chapter 52" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="motif/animals,motif/bells,motif/city,motif/clock,motif/flag,motif/night,motif/time,concept/body,concept/hope,concept/union,character/barnaby_rudge,character/sunday"></span>


Chapter 52


A mob is usually a creature of very mysterious existence, particularly
in a large [[motifs/city|city]]. Where it comes from or whither it goes, few men
can tell. Assembling and dispersing with equal suddenness, it is as
difficult to follow to its various sources as the sea itself; nor does
the parallel stop here, for the ocean is not more fickle and uncertain,
more terrible when roused, more unreasonable, or more cruel.

The people who were boisterous at Westminster upon the Friday morning,
and were eagerly bent upon the work of devastation in Duke Street and
Warwick Street at [[motifs/night|night]], were, in the mass, the same. Allowing for the
chance accessions of which any crowd is morally sure in a town where
there must always be a large number of idle and profligate persons,
one and the same mob was at both places. Yet they spread themselves
in various directions when they dispersed in the afternoon, made no
appointment for reassembling, had no definite purpose or design, and
indeed, for anything they knew, were scattered beyond the [[concepts/hope|hope]] of future
[[concepts/union|union]].

At The Boot, which, as has been shown, was in a manner the head-quarters
of the rioters, there were not, upon this Friday [[motifs/night|night]], a dozen people.
Some slept in the stable and outhouses, some in the common room, some
two or three in beds. The rest were in their usual homes or haunts.
Perhaps not a score in all lay in the adjacent fields and lanes, and
under haystacks, or near the warmth of brick-kilns, who had not their
accustomed place of rest beneath the open sky. As to the public ways
within the town, they had their ordinary nightly occupants, and no
others; the usual amount of vice and wretchedness, but no more.

The experience of one evening, however, had taught the reckless leaders
of disturbance, that they had but to show themselves in the streets, to
be immediately surrounded by materials which they could only have kept
together when their aid was not required, at great risk, expense, and
trouble. Once possessed of this secret, they were as confident as if
twenty thousand men, devoted to their will, had been encamped about
them, and assumed a confidence which could not have been surpassed,
though that had really been the case. All day, Saturday, they remained
quiet. On [[characters/sunday|Sunday]], they rather studied how to keep their men within call,
and in full [[concepts/hope|hope]], than to follow out, by any fierce measure, their first
day’s proceedings.

‘I [[concepts/hope|hope]],’ said Dennis, as, with a loud yawn, he raised his [[concepts/body|body]] from
a heap of straw on which he had been sleeping, and supporting his head
upon his hand, appealed to Hugh on [[characters/sunday|Sunday]] morning, ‘that Muster Gashford
allows some rest? Perhaps he’d have us at work again already, eh?’

‘It’s not his way to let matters drop, you may be sure of that,’ growled
Hugh in answer. ‘I’m in no humour to stir yet, though. I’m as stiff as
a dead [[concepts/body|body]], and as full of ugly scratches as if I had been fighting all
day yesterday with wild cats.’

‘You’ve so much enthusiasm, that’s it,’ said Dennis, looking with great
admiration at the uncombed head, matted beard, and torn hands and face
of the wild figure before him; ‘you’re such a devil of a fellow. You
hurt yourself a hundred times more than you need, because you will be
foremost in everything, and will do more than the rest.’

‘For the matter of that,’ returned Hugh, shaking back his ragged hair
and glancing towards the door of the stable in which they lay; ‘there’s
one yonder as good as me. What did I tell you about him? Did I say he
was worth a dozen, when you doubted him?’

Mr Dennis rolled lazily over upon his breast, and resting his chin upon
his hand in imitation of the attitude in which Hugh lay, said, as he too
looked towards the door:

‘Ay, ay, you knew him, brother, you knew him. But who’d suppose to look
at that chap now, that he could be the man he is! Isn’t it a thousand
cruel pities, brother, that instead of taking his nat’ral rest and
qualifying himself for further exertions in this here honourable cause,
he should be playing at soldiers like a boy? And his cleanliness too!’
said Mr Dennis, who certainly had no reason to entertain a fellow
feeling with anybody who was particular on that score; ‘what weaknesses
he’s guilty of; with respect to his cleanliness! At five o’[[motifs/clock|clock]] this
morning, there he was at the pump, though any one would think he had
gone through enough, the day before yesterday, to be pretty fast asleep
at that [[motifs/time|time]]. But no--when I woke for a minute or two, there he was at
the pump, and if you’d seen him sticking them peacock’s feathers into
his hat when he’d done washing--ah! I’m sorry he’s such a imperfect
character, but the best on us is incomplete in some pint of view or
another.’

The subject of this dialogue and of these concluding remarks, which were
uttered in a tone of philosophical meditation, was, as the reader will
have divined, no other than Barnaby, who, with his [[motifs/flag|flag]] in hand, stood
sentry in the little patch of sunlight at the distant door, or walked
to and fro outside, singing softly to himself; and keeping [[motifs/time|time]] to the
music of some clear church [[motifs/bells|bells]]. Whether he stood still, leaning with
both hands on the flagstaff, or, bearing it upon his shoulder, paced
slowly up and down, the careful arrangement of his poor dress, and his
erect and lofty bearing, showed how high a sense he had of the great
importance of his trust, and how happy and how proud it made him. To
Hugh and his companion, who lay in a dark corner of the gloomy shed,
he, and the sunlight, and the peaceful Sabbath sound to which he made
response, seemed like a bright picture framed by the door, and set
off by the stable’s blackness. The whole formed such a contrast to
themselves, as they lay wallowing, like some obscene [[motifs/animals|animals]], in their
squalor and wickedness on the two heaps of straw, that for a few moments
they looked on without speaking, and felt almost ashamed.


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

Capitolo 52


Una folla è solitamente una creatura di esistenza molto misteriosa, specialmente in una grande [[motifs/city|città]]. Da dove proviene o dove va, pochi uomini possono saperlo. Si raduna e si disperde con la stessa rapidità; è altrettanto difficile rintracciare le sue origini quanto seguire il corso del mare stesso. E la somiglianza non finisce qui: l’oceano, infatti, non è meno capriccioso e imprevedibile, né meno terribile quando si scatena la sua furia, né meno irragionevole o crudele.

Le persone che avevano causato tanto trambusto a Westminster quella mattina di venerdì, e che con grande fervore si erano dedicate alle attività di distruzione in Duke Street e Warwick Street di [[motifs/night|notte]], erano per lo più le stesse. Tenendo conto dei nuovi elementi che, in una città dove sempre esiste un gran numero di persone oziose e dissolute, possono aggregarsi a qualsiasi folla, si trattava della stessa banda di teppisti in entrambi i luoghi. Tuttavia, quando si dispersero nel pomeriggio, si diramarono in varie direzioni, senza alcun accordo preciso per riunirsi nuovamente, senza un obiettivo o una strategia definiti; anzi, per quel che ne sapevano loro, erano ormai così dispersi da rendere impossibile qualsiasi futura [[concepts/union|riunione]].

Al “The Boot”, che, come è stato dimostrato, fungeva in un certo senso da quartier generale dei rivoltosi, quella [[motifs/night|notte]] di venerdì non c'erano nemmeno una dozzina di persone. Alcune dormivano nella stalla e nelle stanze esterne, altre nella sala comune, alcune in letti singoli o in piccoli gruppi. Le restanti si trovavano nelle loro abitazioni o nei luoghi abituali. Forse non c'erano nemmeno venti persone in tutto nei campi circostanti, sotto i mucchi di fieno o vicino ai forni per la cottura dei mattoni: tutti avevano il proprio solito posto dove riposare, all’aperto. Per quanto riguarda le strade della città, esse erano occupate dai soliti frequentatori notturni, e nessun altro; c’era la solita quantità di vizi e miseria, ma nient’altro di più.

Tuttavia, l’esperienza di quella sera insegnò ai capi sconsiderati dei disordini che bastava loro comparire per strada perché subito venissero circondati da risorse che avrebbero potuto mantenere solo con grande rischio, spesa e difficoltà, quando non erano necessarie. Una volta conosciuta questa verità, si sentirono così sicuri come se ventimila uomini fedeli alla loro volontà fossero accampati intorno a loro, e assunsero un’arroganza che nessuno avrebbe potuto eguagliare, anche se in realtà non era affatto così. Per tutto il sabato rimasero tranquilli; la [[characters/sunday|domenica]], invece, si concentrarono soprattutto sul modo per tenere i loro uomini pronti all’azione, piuttosto che ricorrere a misure drastiche come il giorno precedente.

“Spero,” disse Dennis, mentre con un grande sbadiglio si alzava da un mucchio di paglia su cui aveva dormito, appoggiandosi la testa sulla mano, e rivolgendosi a Hugh una domanda il [[characters/sunday|domenica]] mattina: “Che Muster Gashford ci permetta di riposare un po’, no? Forse già ci avrà fatto tornare al lavoro, eh?”

“Non è nel suo carattere lasciare le cose come stanno, di questo puoi essere sicuro,” ringhiò Hugh in risposta. “Però al momento non ho affatto voglia di muovermi. Sono rigido come un cadavere e pieno di brutti graffi, come se ieri intera la giornata avessi combattuto con gatti selvatici.”

“Hai così tanto entusiasmo, è proprio questo che ti caratterizza,” disse Dennis, guardando con grande ammirazione quella figura selvaggia davanti a lui: i capelli disordinati, la barba arruffata, le mani e il viso graffiati. “Sei davvero un tipo straordinario. Ti ferisci cento volte più del necessario, perché vuoi sempre essere il primo in tutto e fare di più degli altri.”

“Per quanto riguarda questo,” rispose Hugh, scuotendo i suoi capelli arruffati e guardando verso la porta dello stallo in cui si trovavano; “ce n’è uno là che è altrettanto bravo di me. Cosa vi avevo detto di lui? Vi ho detto che valeva una dozzina, quando ne dubitavate, vero?”

Il signor Dennis si girò pigramente sul petto, appoggiando il mento sulla mano, imitando l’atteggiamento di Hugh, e disse, guardando anche lui verso la porta:

“Ah, ah. Lo conoscevi bene, fratello. Ma chi avrebbe mai pensato che quel ragazzo potesse diventare l’uomo che è ora! Non è davvero una grande tragedia, fratello? Invece di riposarsi e prepararsi a continuare a impegnarsi in questa nobile causa, si comporta come un bambino che gioca a soldatini. E poi, quella sua mancanza di pulizia, ” disse il signor Dennis, che certamente non aveva alcun motivo per provare simpatia per chi era così rigido su queste questioni; “Che debolezze. Quella sua mancanza di cura personale! Alle cinque di questa mattina, eccolo già alla fontana. Anche se si potrebbe pensare che il giorno prima avesse già fatto abbastanza da essere profondamente addormentato a quell’ora. Ma no. Quando mi sono svegliato per un attimo, lo ho visto ancora lì. E poi, quando finiva di lavarsi, si metteva persino piume di pavone nel cappello. Ah. Mi dispiace che sia una persona così imperfetta. Ma anche il migliore di noi è incompleto sotto qualche aspetto, ”

L’oggetto di questo dialogo e di queste osservazioni conclusive, pronunciate con tono di meditazione filosofica, non era altri che Barnaby: egli, con la sua [[motifs/flag|-bandiera]] in mano, stava di guardia nel riquadro di luce solare presso la porta lontana, o camminava avanti e indietro all’esterno, cantando sottovoce tra sé, seguendo il ritmo delle chiare note delle [[motifs/bells|campane]] della chiesa. Che stesse fermo, appoggiato con entrambe le mani al palo della bandiera, oppure la portasse sulle spalle camminando lentamente avanti e indietro, l’accurata cura con cui aveva sistemato i propri poveri abiti, nonché il suo portamento eretto e maestoso, dimostravano quanto fosse consapevole dell’enorme importanza della fiducia che gli era stata affidata, e quanto ciò lo rendesse felice e orgoglioso. Per Hugh e il suo compagno, che giacevano in un angolo buio del capanno oscuro, lui, la luce solare e quei suoni tranquilli del sabato a cui rispondeva sembravano una bella immagine incorniciata dalla porta e messa in risalto dall’oscurità dello stallo. Tutto ciò formava un contrasto così marcato rispetto alla loro condizione miserabile – giacevano infatti nel loro sporco e nella loro malvagità, tra due mucchi di paglia – che per qualche momento rimasero a guardare in silenzio, provando quasi vergogna.



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_52--part_02" data-title="Barnaby Rudge — Chapter 52 (part 2)" data-chapter="Chapter 52" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="archetype/innocent,motif/dust,motif/grave,motif/lion,motif/night,motif/time,motif/water,motif/well,concept/body,concept/honour,concept/wonder,character/barnaby_rudge,character/simon_tappertit,character/sunday"></span>


‘Ah!’ said Hugh at length, carrying it off with a laugh: ‘He’s a rare
fellow is Barnaby, and can do more, with less rest, or meat, or drink,
than any of us. As to his soldiering, I put him on duty there.’

‘Then there was a object in it, and a proper good one too, I’ll be
sworn,’ retorted Dennis with a broad grin, and an oath of the same
quality. ‘What was it, brother?’

‘Why, you see,’ said Hugh, crawling a little nearer to him, ‘that our
noble captain yonder, came in yesterday morning rather the worse for
liquor, and was--like you and me--ditto last [[motifs/night|night]].’

Dennis looked to where [[characters/simon-tappertit|Simon Tappertit]] lay coiled upon a truss of hay,
snoring profoundly, and nodded.

‘And our noble captain,’ continued Hugh with another laugh, ‘our noble
captain and I, have planned for to-morrow a roaring expedition, with
good profit in it.’

‘Again the Papists?’ asked Dennis, rubbing his hands.

‘Ay, against the Papists--against one of ‘em at least, that some of us,
and I for one, owe a good heavy grudge to.’

‘Not Muster Gashford’s friend that he spoke to us about in my house,
eh?’ said Dennis, brimfull of pleasant expectation.

‘The same man,’ said Hugh.

‘That’s your sort,’ cried Mr Dennis, gaily shaking hands with him,
‘that’s the kind of game. Let’s have revenges and injuries, and all
that, and we shall get on twice as fast. Now you talk, indeed!’

‘Ha ha ha! The captain,’ added Hugh, ‘has thoughts of carrying off a
woman in the bustle, and--ha ha ha!--and so have I!’

Mr Dennis received this part of the scheme with a wry face, observing
that as a general principle he objected to women altogether, as being
unsafe and slippery persons on whom there was no calculating with any
certainty, and who were never in the same mind for four-and-twenty hours
at a stretch. He might have expatiated on this suggestive theme at
much greater length, but that it occurred to him to ask what connection
existed between the proposed expedition and Barnaby’s being posted at
the stable-door as sentry; to which Hugh cautiously replied in these
words:

‘Why, the people we mean to visit, were friends of his, once upon a
[[motifs/time|time]], and I know that much of him to feel pretty sure that if he thought
we were going to do them any harm, he’d be no friend to our side, but
would lend a ready hand to the other. So I’ve persuaded him (for I know
him of old) that Lord George has picked him out to guard this place
to-morrow while we’re away, and that it’s a great [[concepts/honour|honour]]--and so he’s on
duty now, and as proud of it as if he was a general. Ha ha! What do you
say to me for a careful man as [[motifs/well|well]] as a devil of a one?’

Mr Dennis exhausted himself in compliments, and then added,

‘But about the expedition itself--’

‘About that,’ said Hugh, ‘you shall hear all particulars from me and
the great captain conjointly and both together--for see, he’s waking up.
Rouse yourself, [[motifs/lion|lion]]-heart. Ha ha! Put a good face upon it, and drink
again. Another hair of the dog that bit you, captain! Call for
drink! There’s enough of gold and silver cups and candlesticks buried
underneath my bed,’ he added, rolling back the straw, and pointing to
where the ground was newly turned, ‘to pay for it, if it was a score of
casks full. Drink, captain!’

Mr Tappertit received these jovial promptings with a very bad grace,
being much the worse, both in mind and [[concepts/body|body]], for his two nights of
debauch, and but indifferently able to stand upon his legs. With Hugh’s
assistance, however, he contrived to stagger to the pump; and having
refreshed himself with an abundant draught of cold [[motifs/water|water]], and a copious
shower of the same refreshing liquid on his head and face, he ordered
some rum and milk to be served; and upon that [[archetypes/innocent|innocent]] beverage and some
biscuits and cheese made a pretty hearty meal. That done, he disposed
himself in an easy attitude on the ground beside his two companions (who
were carousing after their own tastes), and proceeded to enlighten Mr
Dennis in reference to to-morrow’s project.

That their conversation was an interesting one, was rendered manifest by
its length, and by the close attention of all three. That it was not
of an oppressively [[motifs/grave|grave]] character, but was enlivened by various
pleasantries arising out of the subject, was clear from their loud and
frequent roars of laughter, which startled Barnaby on his post, and made
him [[concepts/wonder|wonder]] at their levity. But he was not summoned to join them, until
they had eaten, and drunk, and slept, and talked together for some
hours; not, indeed, until the twilight; when they informed him that they
were about to make a slight demonstration in the streets--just to keep
the people’s hands in, as it was [[characters/sunday|Sunday]] [[motifs/night|night]], and the public might
otherwise be disappointed--and that he was free to accompany them if he
would.

Without the slightest preparation, saving that they carried clubs and
wore the blue cockade, they sallied out into the streets; and, with no
more settled design than that of doing as much mischief as they could,
paraded them at random. Their numbers rapidly increasing, they soon
divided into parties; and agreeing to meet by-and-by, in the fields
near Welbeck Street, scoured the town in various directions. The largest
[[concepts/body|body]], and that which augmented with the greatest rapidity, was the
one to which Hugh and Barnaby belonged. This took its way towards
Moorfields, where there was a rich chapel, and in which neighbourhood
several Catholic families were known to reside.

Beginning with the private houses so occupied, they broke open the doors
and windows; and while they destroyed the furniture and left but the
bare walls, made a sharp search for tools and engines of destruction,
such as hammers, pokers, axes, saws, and such like instruments. Many of
the rioters made belts of cord, of handkerchiefs, or any material they
found at hand, and wore these weapons as openly as pioneers upon a
field-day. There was not the least disguise or concealment--indeed, on
this [[motifs/night|night]], very little excitement or hurry. From the chapels, they
tore down and took away the very altars, benches, pulpits, pews, and
flooring; from the dwelling-houses, the very wainscoting and stairs.
This [[characters/sunday|Sunday]] evening’s recreation they pursued like mere workmen who had
a certain task to do, and did it. Fifty resolute men might have turned
them at any moment; a single company of soldiers could have scattered
them like [[motifs/dust|dust]]; but no man interposed, no authority restrained them,
and, except by the terrified persons who fled from their approach, they
were as little heeded as if they were pursuing their lawful occupations
with the utmost sobriety and good conduct.

In the same manner, they marched to the place of rendezvous agreed upon,
made great fires in the fields, and reserving the most valuable of their
spoils, burnt the rest. Priestly garments, images of saints, rich stuffs
and ornaments, altar-furniture and household goods, were cast into the
flames, and shed a glare on the whole country round; but they danced
and howled, and roared about these fires till they were tired, and were
never for an instant checked.

As the main [[concepts/body|body]] filed off from this scene of action, and passed down
Welbeck Street, they came upon Gashford, who had been a witness of their
proceedings, and was walking stealthily along the pavement. Keeping up
with him, and yet not seeming to speak, Hugh muttered in his ear:

‘Is this better, master?’

‘No,’ said Gashford. ‘It is not.’

‘What would you have?’ said Hugh. ‘Fevers are never at their height at
once. They must get on by degrees.’

‘I would have you,’ said Gashford, pinching his arm with such
malevolence that his nails seemed to meet in the skin; ‘I would have you
put some meaning into your work. Fools! Can you make no better bonfires
than of rags and scraps? Can you burn nothing whole?’

‘A little patience, master,’ said Hugh. ‘Wait but a few hours, and you
shall see. Look for a redness in the sky, to-morrow [[motifs/night|night]].’

With that, he fell back into his place beside Barnaby; and when the
secretary looked after him, both were lost in the crowd.




<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_53--part_01" data-title="Barnaby Rudge — Chapter 53 (part 1)" data-chapter="Chapter 53" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="archetype/king,motif/bells,motif/city,motif/clock,motif/cross,motif/home,motif/lamb,motif/love,motif/night,motif/time,motif/well,concept/doubt,concept/honour,concept/hope,concept/madness,concept/poverty,concept/self,character/barnaby_rudge"></span>


Chapter 53


The next day was ushered in by merry peals of [[motifs/bells|bells]], and by the firing
of the Tower guns; flags were hoisted on many of the church-steeples;
the usual demonstrations were made in [[concepts/honour|honour]] of the anniversary of the
[[archetypes/king|King]]’s birthday; and every man went about his pleasure or business as
if the [[motifs/city|city]] were in perfect order, and there were no half-smouldering
embers in its secret places, which, on the approach of [[motifs/night|night]], would
kindle up again and scatter ruin and dismay abroad. The leaders of the
riot, rendered still more daring by the success of last [[motifs/night|night]] and by
the booty they had acquired, kept steadily together, and only thought of
implicating the mass of their followers so deeply that no [[concepts/hope|hope]] of pardon
or reward might tempt them to betray their more notorious confederates
into the hands of justice.

Indeed, the sense of having gone too far to be forgiven, held the timid
together no less than the bold. Many who would readily have pointed out
the foremost rioters and given evidence against them, felt that escape
by that means was hopeless, when their every act had been observed by
scores of people who had taken no part in the disturbances; who had
suffered in their persons, peace, or property, by the outrages of the
mob; who would be most willing witnesses; and whom the government would,
no [[concepts/doubt|doubt]], prefer to any [[archetypes/king|King]]’s evidence that might be offered. Many of
this class had deserted their usual occupations on the Saturday morning;
some had been seen by their employers active in the tumult; others
knew they must be suspected, and that they would be discharged if they
returned; others had been desperate from the beginning, and comforted
themselves with the homely proverb, that, being hanged at all, they
might as [[motifs/well|well]] be hanged for a sheep as a [[motifs/lamb|lamb]]. They all hoped and
believed, in a greater or less degree, that the government they seemed
to have paralysed, would, in its terror, come to terms with them in the
end, and suffer them to make their own conditions. The least sanguine
among them reasoned with himself that, at the worst, they were too many
to be all punished, and that he had as good a chance of escape as any
other man. The great mass never reasoned or thought at all, but were
stimulated by their own headlong passions, by [[concepts/poverty|poverty]], by ignorance, by
the [[motifs/love|love]] of mischief, and the [[concepts/hope|hope]] of plunder.

One other circumstance is worthy of remark; and that is, that from the
moment of their first outbreak at Westminster, every symptom of order
or preconcerted arrangement among them vanished. When they divided
into parties and ran to different quarters of the town, it was on the
spontaneous suggestion of the moment. Each party swelled as it went
along, like rivers as they roll towards the sea; new leaders sprang
up as they were wanted, disappeared when the necessity was over, and
reappeared at the next crisis. Each tumult took shape and form from the
circumstances of the moment; sober workmen, going [[motifs/home|home]] from their day’s
labour, were seen to cast down their baskets of tools and become rioters
in an instant; mere boys on errands did the like. In a word, a moral
plague ran through the [[motifs/city|city]]. The noise, and hurry, and excitement, had
for hundreds and hundreds an attraction they had no firmness to resist.
The contagion spread like a dread fever: an infectious [[concepts/madness|madness]], as yet
not near its height, seized on new victims every hour, and society began
to tremble at their ravings.

It was between two and three o’[[motifs/clock|clock]] in the afternoon when Gashford
looked into the lair described in the last chapter, and seeing only
Barnaby and Dennis there, inquired for Hugh.

He was out, Barnaby told him; had gone out more than an hour ago; and
had not yet returned.

‘Dennis!’ said the smiling secretary, in his smoothest voice, as he sat
down [[motifs/cross|cross]]-legged on a barrel, ‘Dennis!’

The hangman struggled into a sitting posture directly, and with his eyes
wide open, looked towards him.

‘How do you do, Dennis?’ said Gashford, nodding. ‘I [[concepts/hope|hope]] you have
suffered no inconvenience from your late exertions, Dennis?’

‘I always will say of you, Muster Gashford,’ returned the hangman,
staring at him, ‘that that ‘ere quiet way of yours might almost wake a
dead man. It is,’ he added, with a muttered oath--still staring at him
in a thoughtful manner--‘so awful sly!’

‘So distinct, eh Dennis?’

‘Distinct!’ he answered, scratching his head, and keeping his eyes upon
the secretary’s face; ‘I seem to hear it, Muster Gashford, in my wery
bones.’

‘I am very glad your sense of hearing is so sharp, and that I succeed
in making myself so intelligible,’ said Gashford, in his unvarying, even
tone. ‘Where is your friend?’

Mr Dennis looked round as in expectation of beholding him asleep upon
his bed of straw; then remembering he had seen him go out, replied:

‘I can’t say where he is, Muster Gashford, I expected him back afore
now. I [[concepts/hope|hope]] it isn’t [[motifs/time|time]] that we was busy, Muster Gashford?’

‘Nay,’ said the secretary, ‘who should know that as [[motifs/well|well]] as you? How
can I tell you, Dennis? You are perfect master of your own actions, you
know, and accountable to nobody--except sometimes to the law, eh?’

Dennis, who was very much baffled by the cool matter-of-course manner of
this reply, recovered his [[concepts/self|self]]-possession on his professional pursuits
being referred to, and pointing towards Barnaby, shook his head and
frowned.

‘Hush!’ cried Barnaby.

‘Ah! Do hush about that, Muster Gashford,’ said the hangman in a low
voice, ‘pop’lar prejudices--you always forget--[[motifs/well|well]], Barnaby, my lad,
what’s the matter?’

‘I hear him coming,’ he answered: ‘Hark! Do you mark that? That’s his
foot! Bless you, I know his step, and his dog’s too. Tramp, tramp,
pit-pat, on they come together, and, ha ha ha!--and here they are!’ he
cried, joyfully welcoming Hugh with both hands, and then patting him
fondly on the back, as if instead of being the rough companion he was,
he had been one of the most prepossessing of men. ‘Here he is, and safe
too! I am glad to see him back again, old Hugh!’


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

Capitolo 53


Il giorno seguente iniziò con allegri rintocchi di [[motifs/bells|campane]] e con il fuoco delle artiglierie della Torre; molte guglie delle chiese issarono le bandiere; si tennero le solite celebrazioni in onore dell’anniversario del compleanno del [[archetypes/king|Re]]; e tutti andavano per i fatti loro, come se la [[motifs/city|città]] fosse in perfetto ordine, senza alcun segno di disordine nascosto che, con l’avvicinarsi della [[motifs/night|notte]], avrebbe potuto riaccendersi e causare distruzione e panico. I capi della rivolta, resi ancora più audaci dal successo della scorsa [[motifs/night|notte]] e dai bottini ottenuti, rimasero uniti e pensarono soltanto a coinvolgere il maggior numero possibile dei loro seguaci in modo che nessuna [[concepts/hope|speranza]] di perdono o ricompensa potesse indurli a tradire i loro complici più notori e consegnarli alla giustizia.

Infatti, la sensazione di aver fatto troppo per essere perdonati teneva uniti tanto i timidi quanto i coraggiosi. Molti coloro che avrebbero facilmente potuto indicare i principali responsabili dei disordini e fornire prove contro di loro ritenevano che fuggire in quel modo fosse impossibile, poiché ogni loro azione era stata osservata da molte persone che non avevano partecipato ai tumulti; persone che avevano sofferto personalmente, per la propria pace o proprietà, a causa delle violenze della folla; persone che sarebbero state più che felici di testimoniare contro di loro; e persone che, senza dubbio, il governo avrebbe preferito alle eventuali testimonianze di qualsiasi [[concepts/doubt|re]] potessero essere fornite. Molti di questi individui avevano abbandonato le proprie occupazioni abituali sabato mattina; alcuni erano stati visti dai loro datori di lavoro mentre partecipavano ai disordini; altri sapevano di essere sospettati e che sarebbero stati licenziati se fossero tornati al lavoro; altri ancora erano già disperati fin dall’inizio, e si consolavano con il vecchio detto secondo cui, essendo destinati comunque alla morte per impiccagione, tanto valeva che morissero per una pecora quanto per un agnello. Tutti speravano, in misura maggiore o minore, che il governo che sembrava averli paralizzati, alla fine, spinto dal terrore, avrebbe accettato le loro condizioni. I meno ottimisti tra loro ragionavano che, nel peggiore dei casi, erano troppi per essere tutti puniti, e quindi avevano le stesse possibilità di scappare degli altri. La grande maggioranza, invece, non ragionava affatto; veniva spinta soltanto dalle proprie passioni irrefrenabili, dalla [[concepts/poverty|povertà]], dall’ignoranza, dal desiderio di causare problemi e dalla speranza di ottenere bottini.

Un'altra circostanza merita di essere menzionata: da quel momento in cui i primi disordini scoppiarono a Westminster, ogni traccia di ordine o organizzazione premeditata tra loro scomparve. Quando si divisero in fazioni e si dispersero nelle varie zone della città, fu su spinta spontanea del momento stesso. Ogni fazione si ingrandiva man mano che avanzava, come i fiumi che scorrono verso il mare; nuovi leader emergevano quando ne era necessario l’uso, scomparivano non appena la loro funzione terminava e ricomparivano durante la crisi successiva. Ogni tumulto prendeva forma in base alle circostanze del momento: onesti lavoratori che tornavano a casa dopo una giornata di fatica si trasformavano all’istante in rivoltosi; persino ragazzi che andavano a fare commissioni facevano lo stesso. In breve, una sorta di “peste morale” dilagò nella città. Il rumore, l’agitazione e l’eccitazione esercitavano su centinaia di persone un fascino al quale era impossibile resistere. La contagiosità si diffondeva come una terribile febbre: una follia contagiosa, che non aveva ancora raggiunto il suo apice, colpiva nuove vittime ogni ora, e la società iniziava a tremare di fronte ai loro atti distruttivi.

Era tra le due e le tre del pomeriggio quando Gashford guardò nella tana descritta nel capitolo precedente e, vedendo lì solo Barnaby e Dennis, chiese di Hugh.

Era uscito, gli disse Barnaby; era andato via più di un’ora prima e non era ancora tornato.

“Dennis!” disse la segretaria sorridente, con la sua voce più dolce, mentre si sedeva con le gambe incrociate su un barile. “Dennis!”

L’impiccatore riuscì a mettersi a sedere di scatto; con gli occhi spalancati, lo guardò direttamente.

“Come sta, Dennis?” disse Gashford annuendo. “Spero che non abbia sofferto alcun inconveniente a causa degli sforzi fatti di recente, Dennis, ”

“Sempre dirò di te, Muster Gashford,” rispose il boia, fissandolo, “che quel tuo modo così tranquillo potrebbe quasi svegliare un morto. È davvero, ” aggiunse, mormorando una bestemmia mentre continuava a guardarlo con aria pensierosa, “così terribilmente astuto!”

“Così diversi, vero, Dennis?”

“Distinto!” rispose, grattandosi la testa e fissando il viso del segretario; “Sembra che lo senta davvero, Mastro Gashford, nelle mie stesse ossa.”

“Sono molto contento che la tua capacità uditiva sia così acuta, e che riesca a farmi capire così bene,” disse Gashford, con il suo solito tono uniforme e pacato. “Dove è tuo amico?”

Il signor Dennis guardò intorno, aspettandosi di vederlo addormentato sul suo letto di paglia; poi, ricordando di averlo visto uscire, rispose:

“Non posso dire dove si trovi, Sergente Gashford. Mi aspettavo che tornasse prima d’ora. Spero che non sia arrivato il momento in cui dovremmo occuparci di altre cose, Sergente Gashford, ”

“No,” disse il segretario, “chi potrebbe saperlo meglio di te? Come posso dirtelo, Dennis? Tu sei il perfetto padrone delle tue azioni, lo sai, e non devi rendere conto a nessuno, tranne, a volte, alla legge, eh?”

Dennis, molto perplesso dal tono disinvolto e naturale di quella risposta, riacquistò la propria calma quando si trattò di questioni professionali. Indicando poi Barnaby, scosse la testa e fece una smorfia.

“Zitti!” gridò Barnaby.

“Ah! State zitto su questo argomento, Muster Gashford,” disse il boia a bassa voce, “quei pregiudizi stupidi. Vi dimenticate sempre, Barnaby, mio ragazzo, di cosa si tratta veramente.”

“Lo sento arrivare,” rispose: “Ascolta! Riconosci quel rumore? Sono i suoi passi. Benedetto te, conosco bene il suo modo di camminare, e anche quello del suo cane. Tic-tac, tic-tac. Arrivano insieme, e, ahahah! Ecco che sono qui!” esclamò, accogliendo Hugh con entrambe le mani pieno di gioia, poi gli diede affettuosamente una pacca sulla schiena, come se invece di essere quel compagno un po’ ruvido, fosse stato uno degli uomini più affascinanti che ci fossero. “Eccolo qui, e anche sano e salvo! Sono felice di rivederlo, vecchio Hugh!”



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_53--part_02" data-title="Barnaby Rudge — Chapter 53 (part 2)" data-chapter="Chapter 53" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="archetype/king,motif/flag,motif/memory,motif/mirror,motif/night,motif/rose,motif/time,motif/well,concept/body,concept/doubt,concept/friendship,concept/hope,concept/temptation,character/barnaby_rudge"></span>


‘I’m a Turk if he don’t give me a warmer welcome always than any man
of sense,’ said Hugh, shaking hands with him with a kind of ferocious
[[concepts/friendship|friendship]], strange enough to see. ‘How are you, boy?’

‘Hearty!’ cried Barnaby, waving his hat. ‘Ha ha ha! And merry too,
Hugh! And ready to do anything for the good cause, and the right, and
to help the kind, mild, pale-faced gentleman--the lord they used so
ill--eh, Hugh?’

‘Ay!’ returned his friend, dropping his hand, and looking at Gashford
for an instant with a changed expression before he spoke to him. ‘Good
day, master!’

‘And good day to you,’ replied the secretary, nursing his leg.

‘And many good days--whole years of them, I [[concepts/hope|hope]]. You are heated.’

‘So would you have been, master,’ said Hugh, wiping his face, ‘if you’d
been running here as fast as I have.’

‘You know the news, then? Yes, I supposed you would have heard it.’

‘News! what news?’

‘You don’t?’ cried Gashford, raising his eyebrows with an exclamation
of surprise. ‘Dear me! Come; then I AM the first to make you acquainted
with your distinguished position, after all. Do you see the [[archetypes/king|King]]’s Arms
a-top?’ he smilingly asked, as he took a large paper from his pocket,
unfolded it, and held it out for Hugh’s inspection.

‘[[motifs/well|Well]]!’ said Hugh. ‘What’s that to me?’

‘Much. A great deal,’ replied the secretary. ‘Read it.’

‘I told you, the first [[motifs/time|time]] I saw you, that I couldn’t read,’ said Hugh,
impatiently. ‘What in the Devil’s name’s inside of it?’

‘It is a proclamation from the [[archetypes/king|King]] in Council,’ said Gashford, ‘dated
to-day, and offering a reward of five hundred pounds--five hundred
pounds is a great deal of money, and a large [[concepts/temptation|temptation]] to some
people--to any one who will discover the person or persons most active
in demolishing those chapels on Saturday [[motifs/night|night]].’

‘Is that all?’ cried Hugh, with an indifferent air. ‘I knew of that.’

‘Truly I might have known you did,’ said Gashford, smiling, and folding
up the document again. ‘Your friend, I might have guessed--indeed I did
guess--was sure to tell you.’

‘My friend!’ stammered Hugh, with an unsuccessful effort to appear
surprised. ‘What friend?’

‘Tut tut--do you suppose I don’t know where you have been?’ retorted
Gashford, rubbing his hands, and beating the back of one on the palm of
the other, and looking at him with a cunning eye. ‘How dull you think
me! Shall I say his name?’

‘No,’ said Hugh, with a hasty glance towards Dennis.

‘You have also heard from him, no [[concepts/doubt|doubt]],’ resumed the secretary, after a
moment’s pause, ‘that the rioters who have been taken (poor fellows) are
committed for trial, and that some very active witnesses have had the
temerity to appear against them. Among others--’ and here he clenched
his teeth, as if he would suppress by force some violent words that [[motifs/rose|rose]]
upon his tongue; and spoke very slowly. ‘Among others, a gentleman
who saw the work going on in Warwick Street; a Catholic gentleman; one
Haredale.’

Hugh would have prevented his uttering the word, but it was out already.
Hearing the name, Barnaby turned swiftly round.

‘Duty, duty, bold Barnaby!’ cried Hugh, assuming his wildest and most
rapid manner, and thrusting into his hand his staff and [[motifs/flag|flag]] which leant
against the wall. ‘Mount guard without loss of [[motifs/time|time]], for we are off upon
our expedition. Up, Dennis, and get ready! Take care that no one turns
the straw upon my bed, brave Barnaby; we know what’s underneath it--eh?
Now, master, quick! What you have to say, say speedily, for the little
captain and a cluster of ‘em are in the fields, and only waiting for us.
Sharp’s the word, and strike’s the action. Quick!’

Barnaby was not proof against this bustle and despatch. The look of
mingled astonishment and anger which had appeared in his face when he
turned towards them, faded from it as the words passed from his [[motifs/memory|memory]],
like breath from a polished [[motifs/mirror|mirror]]; and grasping the weapon which Hugh
forced upon him, he proudly took his station at the door, beyond their
hearing.

‘You might have spoiled our plans, master,’ said Hugh. ‘YOU, too, of all
men!’

‘Who would have supposed that HE would be so quick?’ urged Gashford.

‘He’s as quick sometimes--I don’t mean with his hands, for that you
know, but with his head--as you or any man,’ said Hugh. ‘Dennis, it’s
[[motifs/time|time]] we were going; they’re waiting for us; I came to tell you. Reach
me my stick and belt. Here! Lend a hand, master. Fling this over my
shoulder, and buckle it behind, will you?’

‘Brisk as ever!’ said the secretary, adjusting it for him as he desired.

‘A man need be brisk to-day; there’s brisk work a-foot.’

‘There is, is there?’ said Gashford. He said it with such a provoking
assumption of ignorance, that Hugh, looking over his shoulder and
angrily down upon him, replied:

‘Is there! You know there is! Who knows better than you, master, that
the first great step to be taken is to make examples of these witnesses,
and frighten all men from appearing against us or any of our [[concepts/body|body]], any
more?’

‘There’s one we know of,’ returned Gashford, with an expressive smile,
‘who is at least as [[motifs/well|well]] informed upon that subject as you or I.’

‘If we mean the same gentleman, as I suppose we do,’ Hugh rejoined
softly, ‘I tell you this--he’s as good and quick information about
everything as--’ here he paused and looked round, as if to make sure
that the person in question was not within hearing, ‘as Old Nick
himself. Have you done that, master? How slow you are!’

‘It’s quite fast now,’ said Gashford, rising. ‘I say--you didn’t find
that your friend disapproved of to-day’s little expedition? Ha ha ha!
It is fortunate it jumps so [[motifs/well|well]] with the witness policy; for, once
planned, it must have been carried out. And now you are going, eh?’

‘Now we are going, master!’ Hugh replied. ‘Any parting words?’

‘Oh dear, no,’ said Gashford sweetly. ‘None!’

‘You’re sure?’ cried Hugh, nudging the grinning Dennis.


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

“Sono un turco, se non mi dà sempre una accoglienza più calorosa di qualsiasi altro uomo sano di mente,” disse Hugh, stringendogli la mano con una sorta di ferrea [[concepts/friendship|amicizia]], strana, a dire il vero. “Come stai, ragazzo?”

“Che allegria!” esclamò Barnaby, agitando il suo cappello. “Ah ah ah! E anche molto divertente,
Hugh! E sempre pronto a fare qualsiasi cosa per una causa giusta e nobile, per aiutare quel gentiluomo buono, mite e dal viso pallido, quel signore che sono stati così crudeli con lui, eh, Hugh?”

“Ah!” rispose il suo amico, lasciando andare la sua mano e guardando Gashford per un istante con un’espressione diversa prima di parlargli. “Buongiorno, padrone!”

“E buon giorno a voi,” rispose il segretario, tenendosi la gamba.

“E molti giorni felici, anni interi, spero. Sei arrabbiato.”

“Anch’io avrei fatto lo stesso, padrone,” disse Hugh, asciugandosi il viso, “se fossi corso qui così velocemente come ho fatto io.”

“Allora conosci la notizia, giusto? Sì, immaginavo che l’avessi già sentita.”

“Notizie! Che notizie?”

“Non lo sai?” esclamò Gashford, alzando le sopracciglia in segno di sorpresa. “Mio Dio! Allora sono io il primo ad informarti della tua nobile posizione. Vedi le armi del [[archetypes/king|Re]] in cima?” chiese sorridendo, mentre tirava fuori un grande foglio di carta dalla tasca, lo apriva e lo mostrava a Hugh.

“Beh!”, disse Hugh. “Cosa c’entra questo con me?”

“Molto. Molto di più,” rispose il segretario. “Leggilo.”

“Te l’avevo detto, la prima volta che ti ho visto, che non riuscivo a leggerlo,” disse Hugh, impazientemente. “Cosa diavolo c’è dentro?”

“È un proclama del [[archetypes/king|Re]] emesso in Consiglio,” disse Gashford, “datato di oggi e che offre una ricompensa di cinquecento sterline. Cinquecento sterline sono una somma considerevole, e rappresentano una grande [[concepts/temptation|tentazione]] per alcune persone. Per chiunque sia in grado di individuare la o le persone più coinvolte nella distruzione di quelle cappelle sabato sera.”

“È tutto qui?” esclamò Hugh con indifferenza. “Lo sapevo già.”

“Veramente avrei potuto immaginarlo,” disse Gashford sorridendo e ripiegando di nuovo il documento. “Il tuo amico, probabilmente te l’avrebbe detto.”

“Mio amico!”, balbettò Hugh, nel tentativo fallito di sembrare sorpreso. “Quale amico?”

“Tut tut, pensi davvero che non sappia dove sei stato?” ribatté Gashford, strofinandosi le mani e battendone una contro l’altra, mentre lo guardava con occhi astuti. “Che stupido mi consideri! Devo forse dire il suo nome?”

“No,” disse Hugh, lanciando un’occhiata frettolosa verso Dennis.

“Avete anche sentito da lui, senza alcun [[concepts/doubt|>dubbio]]”, riprese il segretario dopo un momento di pausa, “che i rivoltosi che sono stati arrestati (poveri uomini) saranno processati, e che alcuni testimoni molto attivi hanno avuto la sfrontatezza di presentarsi contro di loro. Tra questi, ”, e qui strinse i denti, come se volesse reprimere a forza alcune parole violente che gli erano salite alle labbra; parlò quindi molto lentamente. “Tra questi, un gentiluomo che ha assistito ai fatti avvenuti in Warwick Street; un gentiluomo cattolico, uno di nome Haredale.”

Hugh avrebbe potuto impedirgli di pronunciare quella parola, ma ormai era già stata detta. Sentendo quel nome, Barnaby si girò rapidamente.

“Dovere, dovere, coraggioso Barnaby!” gridò Hugh, assumendo il suo tono più deciso e veloce, e porgendogli il suo bastone e la sua [[motifs/flag|bandiera]] appoggiati al muro. “Monta di guardia senza perdere [[motifs/time|tempo]], perché partiamo subito per l’impresa. Su, Dennis, preparati! Assicurati che nessuno ribalti la paglia sul mio letto, coraggioso Barnaby; sappiamo cosa c’è sotto, eh? Ora, padrone, sbrigati! Quello che hai da dire, dilllo in fretta, il piccolo capitano e gli altri ci stanno aspettando nei campi. Bisogna agire rapidamente, ”

Barnaby non era immune a tutto questo trambusto e affanno. L’espressione di stupore e rabbia che gli era apparsa sul viso quando si era girato verso di loro svanì non appena quelle parole tornarono nella sua [[motifs/memory|memoria]], come un respiro su uno [[motifs/mirror|specchio]] lucido; poi, afferrando l’arma che Hugh gli aveva imposto, prese con orgoglio posizione alla porta, al di là del loro udito.

“Avresti potuto rovinare i nostri piani, padrone,” disse Hugh. “Tu, proprio tu, tra tutte le persone!”

“Chi avrebbe mai pensato che fosse così veloce?”, insistette Gashford.

“A volte è altrettanto veloce. Non intendo dire con le mani, per quello lo sai già, ma con la testa. Proprio come te o qualsiasi altro uomo,” disse Hugh. “Dennis, è [[motifs/time|ora]] di andare; ci stanno aspettando; sono venuto solo per avvisarti. Dammi il mio bastone e la cintura. Ecco! Aiutami un po’, padrone. Mettimi questa cosa sulla spalla e allacciamela, per favore.”

“Come sempre, veloce!” disse il segretario, sistemandolo secondo i suoi desideri.

“Oggi bisogna essere veloci: c’è del lavoro urgente da svolgere.”

“C’è davvero, c’è?” disse Gashford. Lo disse con un tono così provocatorio, come se fingesse di non saperlo, che Hugh, guardandolo da sopra la spalla e con rabbia, rispose:

“C’è davvero! Lo sai bene che c’è! Chi potrebbe saperlo meglio di te, padrone, se non tu stesso? Il primo grande passo da compiere è proprio quello di dare l’esempio con questi testimoni, per spaventare tutti coloro che osassero opporsi a noi o a qualsiasi membro del nostro [[concepts/body|corpo]].”

“Ne conosciamo uno,” rispose Gashford con un sorriso significativo, “che è almeno altrettanto ben informato su quell’argomento di te o di me.”

“Se ci riferiamo allo stesso gentiluomo, come credo che sia il caso,” riprese Hugh dolcemente, “vi dico questo: è altrettanto affidabile e informato su tutto quanto, come, beh, come Old Nick in persona. L’hai già fatto, padrone? Che lentezza!”

“Ora va abbastanza velocemente,” disse Gashford alzandosi. “Dico, non hai notato che il tuo amico non approvava questa piccola spedizione di oggi? Ah ah ah! È fortunato che tutto sia andato così [[motifs/well|bene]] con la politica dei testimoni; perché, una volta pianificata, l’operazione doveva essere portata a termine. E ora te ne vai, eh?”

“Ora possiamo andare, padrone!” rispose Hugh. “Qualche parola d’addio?”

“Oh no, davvero,” disse Gashford con dolcezza. “Nessuno!”

“Sei sicuro?” gridò Hugh, spingendo il sorridente Dennis.



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_53--part_03" data-title="Barnaby Rudge — Chapter 53 (part 3)" data-chapter="Chapter 53" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="motif/clock,motif/fire,motif/night,motif/sleep,motif/summer,motif/time,motif/well,motif/window,concept/body,concept/mercy,character/barnaby_rudge,character/lord_george_gordon,character/simon_tappertit"></span>


‘Quite sure, eh, Muster Gashford?’ chuckled the hangman.

Gashford paused a moment, struggling with his caution and his malice;
then putting himself between the two men, and laying a hand upon the arm
of each, said, in a cramped whisper:

‘Do not, my good friends--I am sure you will not--forget our talk one
[[motifs/night|night]]--in your house, Dennis--about this person. No [[concepts/mercy|mercy]], no quarter,
no two beams of his house to be left standing where the builder placed
them! [[motifs/fire|Fire]], the saying goes, is a good servant, but a bad master. Make
it _his_ master; he deserves no better. But I am sure you will be firm, I
am sure you will be very resolute, I am sure you will remember that he
thirsts for your lives, and those of all your brave companions. If
you ever acted like staunch fellows, you will do so to-day. Won’t you,
Dennis--won’t you, Hugh?’

The two looked at him, and at each other; then bursting into a roar of
laughter, brandished their staves above their heads, shook hands, and
hurried out.

When they had been gone a little [[motifs/time|time]], Gashford followed. They were yet
in sight, and hastening to that part of the adjacent fields in
which their fellows had already mustered; Hugh was looking back, and
flourishing his hat to Barnaby, who, delighted with his trust, replied
in the same way, and then resumed his pacing up and down before the
stable-door, where his feet had worn a path already. And when Gashford
himself was far distant, and looked back for the last [[motifs/time|time]], he was still
walking to and fro, with the same measured tread; the most devoted and
the blithest champion that ever maintained a post, and felt his heart
lifted up with a brave sense of duty, and determination to defend it to
the last.

Smiling at the simplicity of the poor idiot, Gashford betook himself to
Welbeck Street by a different path from that which he knew the rioters
would take, and sitting down behind a curtain in one of the upper
windows of [[characters/lord-george-gordon|Lord George Gordon]]’s house, waited impatiently for their
coming. They were so long, that although he knew it had been settled
they should come that way, he had a misgiving they must have changed
their plans and taken some other route. But at length the roar of voices
was heard in the neighbouring fields, and soon afterwards they came
thronging past, in a great [[concepts/body|body]].

However, they were not all, nor nearly all, in one [[concepts/body|body]], but were, as he
soon found, divided into four parties, each of which stopped before the
house to give three cheers, and then went on; the leaders crying out in
what direction they were going, and calling on the spectators to join
them. The first detachment, carrying, by way of banners, some relics
of the havoc they had made in Moorfields, proclaimed that they were on
their way to Chelsea, whence they would return in the same order, to
make of the spoil they bore, a great bonfire, near at hand. The second
gave out that they were bound for Wapping, to destroy a chapel; the
third, that their place of destination was East Smithfield, and their
object the same. All this was done in broad, bright, [[motifs/summer|summer]] day. Gay
carriages and chairs stopped to let them pass, or turned back to avoid
them; people on foot stood aside in doorways, or perhaps knocked and
begged permission to stand at a [[motifs/window|window]], or in the hall, until the
rioters had passed: but nobody interfered with them; and when they had
gone by, everything went on as usual.

There still remained the fourth [[concepts/body|body]], and for that the secretary looked
with a most intense eagerness. At last it came up. It was numerous, and
composed of picked men; for as he gazed down among them, he recognised
many upturned faces which he knew [[motifs/well|well]]--those of [[characters/simon-tappertit|Simon Tappertit]], Hugh,
and Dennis in the front, of course. They halted and cheered, as the
others had done; but when they moved again, they did not, like them,
proclaim what design they had. Hugh merely raised his hat upon the
bludgeon he carried, and glancing at a spectator on the opposite side of
the way, was gone.

Gashford followed the direction of his glance instinctively, and
saw, standing on the pavement, and wearing the blue cockade, Sir John
Chester. He held his hat an inch or two above his head, to propitiate
the mob; and, resting gracefully on his cane, smiling pleasantly, and
displaying his dress and person to the very best advantage, looked on
